newsitem.title: FRANCE: French government approves anti-poverty plan.
newsitem.headline: French government approves anti-poverty plan.

text.p: The French government on Wednesday approved a plan to fight poverty by creating jobs for welfare recipients and building more subsidised housing.

The draft legislation, adopted at the weekly cabinet meeting for later submission to parliament, proposes the creation of 300,000 minimum-wage jobs for people receiving state welfare benefits. It would aim to introduce the first 55,000 jobs by the end of the year.

The state would subsidise half of the wages for the first five years to "give the worker the stability required to acquire a skill...and to remain a part of the professional world," said Labour Minister Jacques Barrot.
Young people would be tracked individually to ensure continuity in their professional training.

"This bill shows we are moving from a system of dependency to a system of responsibility because it transforms state aid into working wages," President Jacques Chirac told the cabinet, according to government spokesman Alain Lamassoure.
"When social issues are concerned, it's not always necessary to spend more, but to spend more efficiently," Chirac said.

The package of measures, which would cost an estimated 2.5 billion francs ($450 million), is intended to deliver on Chirac's campaign pledge to fight social exclusion and boost the government's flagging popularity in the face of 12.7 percent unemployment.
The opposition Socialists criticised the bill as not going far enough and providing too little money.

"We are faced with legislation that is more show than real action," said Elisabeth Guigou, the Socialist leader for social affairs told reporters. "The financing is definitely not enough for the stated goals."
Guigou said it took the government 21 months to come up with anti-poverty legislation "although Jacques Chirac made it one of the central points of his campaign".

The legislation also would provide for construction of 100,000 subsidised dwellings over the next five years, reform the way government housing is distributed to give priority to those most in need and allow vacant private as well as public housing to be requisitioned to house the homeless.
The homeless would also be encouraged to register at social services agencies so they could be assured of the right to vote.
